main.summary: The Thousand Character Classic uses one thousand different characters in order to introduce the heavens and earth, the ancient kings, the cultivation of the self, the capitals and palaces, famous people of history, mountains, rivers and products, farming and a life of withdrawal, and it closes on learning and self-discipline. It was both a primer for learning to read and a favourite text for calligraphers to copy again and again.
main.translation:
Heaven is dark and earth is yellow; space and time are vast and primeval.
The sun and moon wax, wane and slant; the stars and constellations are set out in rows.
Cold comes and heat goes; in autumn we reap, in winter we store.
Leap days make up the year; the pitch-pipes tune the yang.
Clouds rise and bring rain; dew gathers and turns to frost.
Gold comes from Lishui; jade comes from the Kunlun ridges.
The sword is named Juque; the pearl is called Night Glow.
Of fruits the plum and the crab-apple are prized; of vegetables mustard greens and ginger count most.
The sea is salty and rivers are fresh; fish dive and birds fly.
The Dragon Master and the Fire Emperor, the Bird Officer and the Human Sovereign.
They began to make writing, and then to wear coats and skirts.
Yielding the throne and giving up the realm: Youyu and Taotang (Shun and Yao).
Comforting the people and punishing the guilty: Fa of Zhou and Tang of Yin.
Sitting in court and asking after the Way, he lets his robes hang and his hands fold, and order is kept.
He loves and rears the black-haired people; the Rong and Qiang tribes submit as vassals.
Near and far are one body; all lead one another to honour the king.
The phoenix cries in the tree; the white colt grazes in the field.
His teaching covers grass and trees; its benefit reaches the ten thousand regions.
This body and these hairs are made of the four elements and the five constants.
We reverently think of our nurture; how dare we damage or harm them?
A woman should admire chastity and purity; a man should follow talent and goodness.
Know a fault and you must mend it; once you have an ability, do not let it go.
Do not speak of others' shortcomings; do not rely on your own strengths.
Let your word be one that can be checked; let your capacity be hard to measure.
Mozi grieved over white silk being dyed; the Songs praised the lambs.
Look up to the bright conduct of the worthy; by steady thought one can become a sage.
When virtue is built, a name is made; when the form is straight, the shadow is true.
In an empty valley a voice carries; in an empty hall one learns to listen.
Calamity comes from piled-up evil; good fortune comes from stored-up goodness.
A foot-wide jade disc is no treasure; an inch of time is what we should strive for.
Serve your father and your lord with seriousness and respect.
Filial piety should use all your strength; loyalty should use up your life.
Walk as if at the edge of a deep pool and on thin ice; rise early and keep your parents warm in winter and cool in summer.
Be fragrant like the orchid, flourishing like the pine.
Be like a river that does not cease; be like a clear pool that gives back a reflection.
Carry yourself as if in thought, and let your speech be steady.
A good beginning is truly fine; a careful ending is better still.
This is the base of glory and achievement, and a good name without end.
With learning to spare, take office; take up a post and take part in government.
While he was in office the people spared the sweet pear tree he sat under; after he left they sang of him all the more.
Music differs for the high and the low; ritual separates the honoured from the humble.
Superiors harmonious, inferiors at peace; the husband leads, the wife follows.
Outside the home, take the teaching of your tutors; inside, follow the example of your mother.
Treat your aunts and uncles, and your nephews and nieces, as close as your own parents and children.
Brothers are deeply cared for: one breath, branches on one bough.
In friendship, share your lot; cut and polish each other with warnings and rules.
Kindness and compassion, pity and sympathy, must not leave you even in haste.
Integrity, rightness, honesty and modesty must not fail even in distress.
Quiet by nature, the feelings are at ease; a restless heart tires the spirit.
Hold to what is true and the will is full; chase after things and the mind drifts.
Keep firmly to a noble conduct, and fine rank will come to you of itself.
The capitals of the Hua and Xia peoples: two cities, east and west.
One with its back to Mount Mang and facing the Luo; the other floating on the Wei and holding the Jing.
Palaces coil and rise in dense clusters; towers and halls soar until they startle.
Birds and beasts are drawn on them, and immortals and spirits painted in colour.
Side halls open beside the main ones; the great tent of the first rank faces the pillars.
Feasts are laid and mats spread; zithers are plucked and reed-organs blown.
As they climb the steps and enter the throne-stair, caps turn and flash like stars.
To the right it reaches the Guangnei hall; to the left it extends to Chengming.
Here they have gathered the ancient books and also assembled the finest talents.
There are Du Du's draft and Zhong Yao's clerical script, writings in lacquer and the classics from the wall.
The offices are filled with generals and ministers; the road is lined with the high ministers of the pagoda-tree rank.
Their households are enfeoffed with eight counties; each family is given a thousand soldiers.
In tall caps they attend the imperial carriage, driving their wheels with tassels swinging.
Their salaries pass down the generations in lavish wealth; their carriages are light and their horses fat.
Their deeds are weighed and recorded, and carved into stele and inscribed.
Jiang Taigong of the Pan stream and Yi Yin helped their age, Yi Yin as the steward Aheng.
The Duke of Zhou was given a seat at Qufu; without Dan, who would have governed it?
Duke Huan of Qi set the lords right and brought them together, rescuing the weak and propping up the fallen.
Qi Liji and others restored the Han emperor Hui; Fu Yue touched the heart of King Wuding.
Men of talent worked tirelessly, and many scholars brought peace.
Jin and Chu in turn were hegemons; Zhao and Wei were hemmed in by the horizontal alliance.
Borrowing a road, one destroyed Guo; at Jiantu a covenant was sworn.
Xiao He followed the simple laws, while Han Fei was ruined by harsh punishments.
Bai Qi, Wang Jian, Lian Po and Li Mu were the finest at handling armies.
They spread their might across the desert, and their fame ran on in painted portraits.
The Nine Provinces hold the footsteps of Yu; the hundred commanderies were joined by Qin.
Of the sacred peaks Heng and Dai are chief; for the feng and shan sacrifices Yunyun and Tingting are the main.
Yanmen and the Purple Frontier; Jitian and Chicheng.
Kunming Lake and Jieshi; Juye and Dongting.
Far and wide, stretching on and on; cliffs and caves, dim and deep.
Government is rooted in farming; devote yourself to sowing and reaping.
Work begins in the south fields, where I plant millet.
Taxes are paid on the ripe crop and first fruits offered; encouragement and reward, demotion and promotion follow.
Mencius was sincere and plain; Shi Yu held to uprightness.
Aim close to the Mean: be diligent, humble, careful and attentive.
Listen to a voice and judge the matter; look at a face and tell the mood.
Leave your descendants good counsel, and urge them to plant with respect.
Examine yourself, and mind the mockery and warnings; as favour grows, resist the limit.
When disgrace and shame draw near, happily one can go to woods and marshes.
The two Shu saw their chance; who forced them to take off their seals?
Living apart in quiet places, silent and still.
Seeking the ancients and weighing their talk, I let my cares scatter and wander free.
Joy rushes in and cares are dismissed; sorrow departs and gladness is invited.
In the pond the lotus is bright and clear; in the garden the weeds put out shoots.
The loquat is green late in the year; the paulownia drops its leaves early.
Old roots lie hidden and covered; fallen leaves flutter and whirl.
A roaming roc flies alone, brushing the crimson sky.
He loved reading, browsed at the market, and let his eyes rest on book-bags and cases.
Careless speech is to be feared; ears may be pressed against the wall.
Prepare the meal and set out the rice: enough to suit the mouth and fill the stomach.
When full, one can enjoy any cooked dish; when hungry, one is not fussy about even dregs and husks.
Relatives and old friends: the old and young eat different food.
Concubines and servants spin and weave; they wait on the towel and the bedchamber.
Silk fans are round and clean; silver candles blaze and glitter.
By day a nap, by night a sleep, on a blue bamboo mat and an ivory bed.
With strings and song and wine feasts, they pass the cup and raise the goblet.
Hands dance and feet stamp, joyful and well.
The heir by the main wife continues the line and takes charge of the winter and autumn sacrifices.
He bows his head to the ground and bows again, awed and afraid.
Letters and notes should be brief and to the point; replies should be careful and full.
When the body is grimy, think of bathing; when you hold something hot, long for coolness.
Donkeys, mules, calves and bulls leap and bound and race.
Execute bandits and thieves; seize rebels and deserters.
Lu Bu shot the halberd; Xiong Yiliao juggled his balls; Ji Kang played the zither, Ruan Ji whistled.
Meng Tian made the brush, Cai Lun the paper, Ma Jun the clever machines, and the Master Ren fished.
They unravelled quarrels and benefited the common folk; all were fine and skilful.
Mao Qiang and Xi Shi were gentle and lovely; even their frowns were skilful, and their smiles beautiful.
The arrows of the years press on every day; the sun's light shines bright.
The jade armillary sphere hangs and turns; the dark of the moon circles and then lights again.
As fire passes from stick to stick of firewood, blessings cultivated are handed on; may peace and good fortune be yours for ever.
Walk with measured steps and lift your chin, bowing up and down in the temple hall.
Bind your belt, dignified and serious; linger and look afar.
One who is ignorant and has heard little is mocked like the foolish and dull.
As for the words called helpers: yan, zai, hu, ye.

keyLines.line: 天地玄黃，宇宙洪荒。日月盈昃，辰宿列張。寒來暑往，秋收冬藏。閏餘成歲，律呂調陽。雲騰致雨，露結為霜。
keyLines.en: Heaven is dark, earth is yellow; space and time are vast and wild. The sun and moon wax and wane; the stars and constellations are set out in rows. Cold comes, heat goes; in autumn we reap, in winter we store. Leap months make up the year; the pitch-pipes tune the yang energy. Clouds rise and bring rain; dew gathers and turns to frost.
keyLines.note: The opening describes the natural world: the sky dark and the earth yellow, the universe wide and primeval, the sun and moon waxing and waning, the stars in their places. Heat and cold alternate, with harvest in autumn and storing in winter. A leap month is added to make the year come out right, and the musical pitches are used to set the yin and yang in tune. Clouds rise and bring rain; dew freezes into frost.

keyLines.line: 金生麗水，玉出崑崗。劍號巨闕，珠稱夜光。果珍李柰，菜重芥薑。海鹹河淡，鱗潛羽翔。
keyLines.en: Gold comes from Lishui; jade comes from the Kunlun ridges. The sword is named Juque; the pearl is called Night Glow. Of fruits the plum and the crab-apple are prized; of vegetables mustard greens and ginger count most. The sea is salty and rivers are fresh; fish dive and birds fly.
keyLines.note: On the products of the land: gold from the Lishui river, fine jade from the Kunlun ridges. A famous sword is Juque and a famous pearl is Night Glow. Plums and crab-apples are the prized fruits, mustard greens and ginger the vegetables that count. The sea is salty and the rivers fresh; fish dive and birds soar.

keyLines.line: 龍師火帝，鳥官人皇。始制文字，乃服衣裳。推位讓國，有虞陶唐。弔民伐罪，周發殷湯。
keyLines.en: The Dragon Master and the Fire Emperor, the Bird Officer and the Human Sovereign. They began to make writing and then to wear coats and skirts. Yielding the throne and giving up the realm: the houses of Youyu and Taotang (Shun and Yao). Comforting the people and punishing the guilty: Fa of Zhou and Tang of Yin.
keyLines.note: On the ancient rulers and the beginnings of civilisation: Fuxi, Shennong, Shaohao and the Human Sovereign, the legendary kings of old. Writing was invented and clothes were made. Yao and Shun passed on the realm by abdication, and King Wu of Zhou, whose name was Ji Fa, and Tang of Shang rose to rescue the people and punish tyrants.

keyLines.line: 坐朝問道，垂拱平章。愛育黎首，臣伏戎羌。遐邇壹體，率賓歸王。鳴鳳在樹，白駒食場。化被草木，賴及萬方。
keyLines.en: Sitting in court and asking after the Way, he lets his robes hang and his hands fold, and order is kept. He loves and rears the black-haired people; the Rong and Qiang tribes submit as vassals. Near and far are one body; all lead one another to honour the king. The phoenix cries in the tree; the white colt grazes in the field. His teaching covers grass and trees; its benefit reaches the ten thousand regions.
keyLines.note: The ideal ruler governs: he sits upright in court seeking the way of good government, and the realm is at peace though he does little. He cares for the common people, and even distant tribes come to submit. Near and far form one body, and every side turns to him. The phoenix and the white colt are at ease, and his teaching reaches the plants and trees and the whole world.

keyLines.line: 蓋此身髮，四大五常。恭惟鞠養，豈敢毀傷。女慕貞絜，男效才良。知過必改，得能莫忘。罔談彼短，靡恃己長。信使可覆，器欲難量。
keyLines.en: This body and these hairs: the four elements and the five constants. We reverently think of our nurture; how dare we damage or harm them? A woman should admire chastity and purity; a man should imitate talent and goodness. Know a fault and you must mend it; once you have an ability, do not let it go. Do not speak of others' shortcomings; do not rely on your own strengths. Let your word be trustworthy and bear checking; let your capacity be so great it is hard to measure.
keyLines.note: Now the lessons for self-cultivation begin: the body is made of the four elements and virtue has five constants. Remembering how heavily parents have nurtured us, we dare not harm even our hair and skin. Women should be chaste and men should follow talent and goodness. Mend faults when you know them and do not forget what you can do. Do not talk of others' faults or lean on your own strengths. Keep your word so it can be tested, and let your breadth of mind be hard to fathom.

keyLines.line: 墨悲絲染，詩讚羔羊。景行維賢，克念作聖。德建名立，形端表正。空谷傳聲，虛堂習聽。禍因惡積，福緣善慶。尺璧非寶，寸陰是競。
keyLines.en: Mozi grieved over white silk dyed; the Songs praised the lambs. Admire the bright conduct of the worthy; by steady thought one can become a sage. When virtue is built, a name is made; when the form is straight, the shadow is true. In an empty valley a voice carries; in an empty hall one learns to listen. Calamity comes from piled-up evil; good fortune comes from stored-up goodness. A foot-wide jade disc is no treasure; an inch of time is what we should strive for.
keyLines.note: Encouragement towards good, and a plea to value time. Mozi sighed at white silk taking on a dye, and the Book of Songs praised the lambs. Look up to the conduct of the worthy, and by keeping it in mind one can become a sage. Where virtue is built, reputation follows. Bad deeds bring calamity sooner or later; good deeds bring happiness. A foot of jade is not a treasure; an inch of time is what is worth striving for.

keyLines.line: 資父事君，曰嚴與敬。孝當竭力，忠則盡命。臨深履薄，夙興溫凊。似蘭斯馨，如松之盛。川流不息，淵澄取映。容止若思，言辭安定。篤初誠美，慎終宜令。
keyLines.en: Serve your father and your lord with respect and reverence, it is said. Filial piety should use all your strength; loyalty should use up your life. Walk as if at the edge of a deep pool and on thin ice; rise early and keep your parents warm in winter and cool in summer. Be fragrant like the orchid, flourishing like the pine. Be like a river that does not cease; be like a clear pool that gives back a reflection. Carry yourself as if in thought, and let your speech be steady. A good beginning is truly fine; a careful ending is better still.
keyLines.note: On filial piety, loyalty and bearing. Serve father and ruler with seriousness and respect: filial piety uses all one's strength and loyalty will give life itself. Act with the care of one at a deep pool's edge or on thin ice, and rise early to see that parents are warm in winter and cool in summer. Let virtue be as fragrant as the orchid, as flourishing as the pine, as unceasing as a river and as clear as a still pool. Move with composure and speak calmly. A good start is admirable, but a careful finish is better.

keyLines.line: 榮業所基，籍甚無竟。學優登仕，攝職從政。存以甘棠，去而益詠。樂殊貴賤，禮別尊卑。上和下睦，夫唱婦隨。
keyLines.en: It is the base of glory and achievement, and a good name that has no end. With learning to spare, take office; take up a post and take part in government. He stayed beneath the sweet pear tree, and after he left the people sang his praises more. Music differs for the high and the low; ritual separates the honoured from the humble. Superiors harmonious, inferiors peaceful; the husband leads, the wife follows.
keyLines.note: On service in government, ritual and music. A good name and great deeds are the foundation of honour, and they never run out. Once learning has more than enough, one takes up office. The Duke of Shao once judged cases under a sweet pear tree, and when he left the people praised him all the more. Music differs by rank, and ritual marks high from low. Those above and below live in harmony, and husband and wife in accord.

keyLines.line: 外受傅訓，入奉母儀。諸姑伯叔，猶子比兒。孔懷兄弟，同氣連枝。交友投分，切磨箴規。仁慈隱惻，造次弗離。節義廉退，顛沛匪虧。
keyLines.en: Outside, take the teaching of your tutors; inside, follow the pattern of your mother. Treat your aunts and uncles, and your nephews and nieces, as you would your own parents and children. Brothers are deeply cared for, one breath, branches on one bough. In friendship, share your lot; cut and polish each other, with warnings and rules. Kindness and compassion, even in haste, must not leave you. Integrity, rightness, honesty and modesty must not fail even in distress.
keyLines.note: On family and friends. Outside the home a young person learns from teachers, and inside from the mother's example. Aunts and uncles are treated like close family, and a nephew like a son. Brothers love each other deeply, being branches of one tree. Friends should share aims and sharpen each other with advice and correction. Kindness and pity should not leave a person even in a hurry; integrity, honesty and modesty should not fail even in hard times.

keyLines.line: 性靜情逸，心動神疲。守真志滿，逐物意移。堅持雅操，好爵自縻。
keyLines.en: Quiet by nature, the feelings are at ease; a restless heart tires the spirit. Hold to what is true and the will is full; chase after things and the mind drifts. Keep firmly to a noble conduct, and fine rank will come to you by itself.
keyLines.note: On self-cultivation. A calm nature gives ease of feeling, and a restless heart wears out the spirit. Hold to what is true and your will is content; chase after outward things and it wavers. Keep to a high standard of conduct and good office will come in its own time.

keyLines.line: 都邑華夏，東西二京。背邙面洛，浮渭據涇。宮殿盤鬱，樓觀飛驚。圖寫禽獸，畫綵仙靈。丙舍傍啟，甲帳對楹。肆筵設席，鼓瑟吹笙。升階納陛，弁轉疑星。
keyLines.en: The capitals of the Hua and Xia peoples: two cities, east and west. One with its back to Mount Mang and facing the Luo; the other floating on the Wei and holding the Jing. Palaces coil and rise in dense clusters; towers and halls soar until they startle. Birds and beasts are painted on them, and immortals and spirits in colour. Side halls open beside the main ones; the great tent of the first rank faces the pillars. Feasts are laid and mats spread; zithers are plucked and reed-organs blown. As they climb the steps and enter the throne-stair, caps turn and flash like stars.
keyLines.note: Now the capital and its palaces. The Chinese heartland has two capitals, Chang'an in the west and Luoyang in the east. Luoyang has the Mang hills behind it and the Luo river in front; Chang'an lies by the Wei and holds the Jing. Palaces wind and gather in great masses, and towers rise to startling heights. Birds, beasts and immortals are painted on the walls in colour. Feasts are laid and music is played, and as officials climb the steps, their caps glitter like stars.

keyLines.line: 右通廣內，左達承明。既集墳典，亦聚群英。杜稿鍾隸，漆書壁經。府羅將相，路俠槐卿。戶封八縣，家給千兵。高冠陪輦，驅轂振纓。世祿侈富，車駕肥輕。策功茂實，勒碑刻銘。
keyLines.en: To the right it reaches the Guangnei hall; to the left it extends to Chengming. Here they have gathered the ancient books and also assembled the finest talents. There are Du Du's draft, Zhong Yao's clerical script, lacquer-ink writings and the classics from the wall. The offices are filled with generals and ministers; the road is flanked by high ministers under the pagoda trees. Their households are enfeoffed with eight counties; each family is given a thousand soldiers. In tall caps they attend the imperial carriage, driving their wheels with tassels swinging. Their salaries pass down the generations in lavish wealth; their carriages are light and their horses fat. Their deeds are weighed and recorded, and carved into stele and inscribed.
keyLines.note: On the court's libraries and its powerful men. To the right is the Guangnei hall of books and to the left the Chengming lodge where court attendants stayed. Ancient texts are collected and the best men gathered. The collection includes Du Du's draft, Zhong Yao's clerical script, writings in lacquer and the classics found in the wall of Confucius's house. The offices are lined with generals and ministers, and the roads with high officials. Their households hold the revenue of eight counties and a thousand soldiers each, and they wear tall caps and follow the emperor's carriage. They enjoy hereditary pay and wealth, and their achievements are carved on stone.

keyLines.line: 磻溪伊尹，佐時阿衡。奄宅曲阜，微旦孰營。桓公匡合，濟弱扶傾。綺回漢惠，說感武丁。俊乂密勿，多士寔寧。
keyLines.en: Jiang Taigong of the Pan stream and Yi Yin helped their age, Yi Yin as the steward Aheng. The Duke of Zhou was given a seat at Qufu; without Dan, who would have governed it? Duke Huan of Qi set the lords right and brought them together, rescuing the weak and propping up the fallen. Qi Liji and others restored the Han emperor Hui; Fu Yue touched the heart of King Wuding. Men of talent worked tirelessly, and many scholars brought peace.
keyLines.note: A roll of good ministers from history: Jiang Taigong fished at the Pan stream, and Yi Yin was honoured as Aheng. The Duke of Zhou (Dan) was enfeoffed at Qufu, and without him no one could have managed it. Duke Huan of Qi rallied the lords and helped the weak. Qi Liji and others secured the throne of Emperor Hui of Han, and Fu Yue was the man King Wuding of Shang had seen in a dream. With such diligent men of talent, the world was at peace.

keyLines.line: 晉楚更霸，趙魏困橫。假途滅虢，踐土會盟。何遵約法，韓弊煩刑。起翦頗牧，用軍最精。宣威沙漠，馳譽丹青。
keyLines.en: Jin and Chu in turn were hegemons; Zhao and Wei were hemmed in by the horizontal alliance. Borrowing a road, one destroyed Guo; at Jiantu a covenant was sworn. Xiao He followed the simple laws, while Han Fei was ruined by harsh punishments. Bai Qi, Wang Jian, Lian Po and Li Mu were the finest at handling armies. They spread their might across the desert, and their fame ran on in painted portraits.
keyLines.note: Events from the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods through to the Han. Jin and Chu took turns as the leading state. Zhao and Wei were squeezed by Qin's horizontal alliance. Jin borrowed a road to destroy Guo, and Duke Wen of Jin made a covenant at Jiantu. Xiao He followed the simple three-article law, while Han Fei died of harsh punishments. Bai Qi, Wang Jian, Lian Po and Li Mu were master generals whose power was felt in the desert and whose portraits carried their fame.

keyLines.line: 九州禹跡，百郡秦并。嶽宗恆岱，禪主云亭。雁門紫塞，雞田赤城。昆池碣石，鉅野洞庭。曠遠綿邈，巖岫杳冥。
keyLines.en: The Nine Provinces hold the footsteps of Yu; the hundred commanderies were joined by Qin. Of the sacred peaks Heng and Dai are chief; for the feng and shan sacrifices Yunyun and Tingting are the main. Yanmen and the Purple Frontier; Jitian and Chicheng. Kunming Lake and Jieshi; Juye and Dongting. Far and wide, stretching on and on; cliffs and caves, dim and deep.
keyLines.note: On geography and mountains and rivers. The Nine Provinces are the land Yu the Great travelled, and the hundred commanderies were put together by Qin. Among the five sacred mountains, Mount Heng and Mount Tai are the greatest, and the feng and shan sacrifices were held at Yunyun and Tingting. Places are named: Yanmen and the Great Wall, Jitian and Chicheng, Kunming Lake, Jieshi, Juye and Lake Dongting. The land is vast and distant, and its caves and cliffs deep.

keyLines.line: 治本於農，務茲稼穡。俶載南畝，我藝黍稷。稅熟貢新，勸賞黜陟。孟軻敦素，史魚秉直。庶幾中庸，勞謙謹敕。聆音察理，鑒貌辨色。貽厥嘉猷，勉其祗植。
keyLines.en: Government is rooted in farming; devote yourself to sowing and reaping. Work begins in the south fields, where I plant millet. Taxes are paid on the ripe crop and first fruits offered; encouragement and reward, demotion and promotion follow. Mencius was sincere and plain; Shi Yu held to uprightness. Aim close to the Mean: be diligent, humble, careful and attentive. Listen to a voice and judge the matter; look at a face and tell the mood. Leave your descendants good counsel, and urge them to plant with respect.
keyLines.note: On farming and character. A state is founded on agriculture, so devote yourself to the crops. The year's work begins in the southern fields with millet. After the harvest, taxes and first fruits are paid, and officials are rewarded or punished, promoted or demoted. Mencius was sincere and plain, Shi Yu upright. Keep close to the Mean and be hard-working, modest and careful. Listen to a voice to understand the matter, and read a face for its mood. Leave good counsel behind, and urge others to cultivate their character with care.

keyLines.line: 省躬譏誡，寵增抗極。殆辱近恥，林皋幸即。兩疏見機，解組誰逼。索居閒處，沉默寂寥。求古尋論，散慮逍遙。
keyLines.en: Examine yourself, and mind the mockery and warnings; as favour grows, resist the limit. When disgrace and shame draw near, happily one can go to woods and marshes. The two Shu saw their chance; who forced them to take off their seals? Living apart in quiet places, silent and still. Seeking the ancients and weighing their talk, I let my cares scatter and wander free.
keyLines.note: On knowing when to stop and withdraw. Reflect on yourself and take criticism as a warning; when favour is greatest, guard against going too far. When danger and disgrace approach, it is fortunate that one can retire to the woods and marshes. The two Shu, uncle and nephew, saw the signs and gave up office without being forced. Living alone in quiet places, silent and still, one reads the ancients and their arguments to disperse worry and roam at ease.

keyLines.line: 欣奏累遣，慼謝歡招。渠荷的歷，園莽抽條。枇杷晚翠，梧桐早凋。陳根委翳，落葉飄颻。遊鵾獨運，凌摩絳霄。
keyLines.en: Joy rushes in and cares are dismissed; sorrow departs and gladness is invited. In the pond the lotus is bright and clear; in the garden the weeds put out shoots. The loquat is green late in the year; the paulownia drops its leaves early. Old roots lie hidden and covered; fallen leaves flutter and whirl. A roaming roc flies alone, brushing the crimson sky.
keyLines.note: On the seasons seen from a quiet retreat. Happiness comes and worries are sent away; sorrow leaves and joy is called in. The lotus in the pond is bright and clear, and in the garden the grass is putting out shoots. The loquat stays green into winter, while the paulownia sheds its leaves early. Old roots are hidden and fallen leaves whirl about. A lone roc flies, rising to touch the red sky.

keyLines.line: 耽讀翫市，寓目囊箱。易輶攸畏，屬耳垣牆。具膳餐飯，適口充腸。飽飫烹宰，飢厭糟糠。親戚故舊，老少異糧。
keyLines.en: He loved reading, browsed at the market, and let his eyes rest on book-bags and cases. Careless speech is to be feared; ears may be pressed against the wall. Prepare the meal and set out the rice: enough to suit the mouth and fill the stomach. When full, one can enjoy any cooked dish; when hungry, one is not fussy about even dregs and husks. Relatives and old friends: the old and young eat different food.
keyLines.note: On reading and eating. He was absorbed in books and looked through them at the market, his eyes resting on the cases of bags and boxes. Careless words bring trouble, so beware of listeners behind the wall. Prepare a simple meal that suits the taste and fills the stomach. A full person can enjoy any dish, but a hungry one will not turn down even coarse dregs. When you host relatives and friends, old and young eat different food.

keyLines.line: 妾御績紡，侍巾帷房。紈扇圓潔，銀燭煒煌。晝眠夕寐，藍筍象床。弦歌酒讌，接杯舉觴。矯手頓足，悅豫且康。
keyLines.en: Concubines and servants spin and weave; they wait on the towel and the bedchamber. Silk fans are round and clean; silver candles blaze and glitter. By day a nap, by night a sleep, on a blue bamboo mat and an ivory bed. With strings and song and wine feasts, they pass the cup and raise the goblet. Hands dance and feet stamp, joyful and well.
keyLines.note: On home life. Concubines and servants spin and weave and wait on the household in the curtained rooms. The round white silk fans are neat and clean; the silver candles shine brightly. People rest by day and sleep by night on bamboo mats and ivory beds. They hold feasts with music and song, pass cups and raise goblets, dancing with hands and feet in joy and good health.

keyLines.line: 嫡後嗣續，祭祀烝嘗。稽顙再拜，悚懼恐惶。牋牒簡要，顧答審詳。骸垢想浴，執熱願涼。驢騾犢特，駭躍超驤。誅斬賊盜，捕獲叛亡。
keyLines.en: The heir by the main wife continues the line and takes charge of the seasonal sacrifices. He bows his head to the ground and bows again, awed and afraid. Letters and notes should be brief and to the point; replies should be careful and full. When the body is grimy, think of bathing; when you hold something hot, long for coolness. Donkeys, mules, calves and bulls leap and bound and race. Execute bandits and thieves; seize rebels and deserters.
keyLines.note: On the family's rites and daily life. The eldest son of the main wife carries on the family and conducts the sacrifices in each season, bowing to the ground twice in reverence and awe. Letters should be short and replies thoughtful. A dirty body longs for a bath, and a hand holding something hot longs for coolness. Donkeys, mules and young cattle start and bound along. Bandits and thieves are put to death and those who rebel or flee are caught.

keyLines.line: 布射遼丸，嵇琴阮嘯。恬筆倫紙，鈞巧任釣。釋紛利俗，並皆佳妙。毛施淑姿，工顰妍笑。
keyLines.en: Lu Bu shot the halberd; Yi Liao juggled his balls; Ji Kang played the zither, Ruan Ji whistled. Meng Tian made the brush, Cai Lun the paper, Ma Jun the clever machines, and the Master Ren fished. They unravelled quarrels and benefited the common folk; all were fine and skilful. Mao Qiang and Xi Shi were gentle and lovely; even their frowns were skilled, and their smiles beautiful.
keyLines.note: On skills and beauties. Lu Bu was a fine archer and Yi Liao a master juggler; Ji Kang played the zither and Ruan Ji could whistle. Meng Tian is credited with the writing brush, Cai Lun with paper, Ma Jun with clever machines and the Master Ren with fishing. They settled disputes and helped ordinary people, and all were admirable. Mao Qiang and Xi Shi were gracious beauties, graceful even when frowning and lovely when smiling.

keyLines.line: 年矢每催，曦暉朗曜。璇璣懸斡，晦魄環照。指薪修祜，永綏吉劭。矩步引領，俯仰廊廟。束帶矜莊，徘徊瞻眺。孤陋寡聞，愚蒙等誚。謂語助者，焉哉乎也。
keyLines.en: The arrows of the years press on every day; the sun's light shines bright. The jade armillary sphere hangs and turns; the dark of the moon circles and then lights again. Pass on the firewood and cultivate blessing; may peace and good fortune be yours for ever. Walk with measured steps and lift your chin, bowing up and down in the temple hall. Bind your belt, dignified and serious; linger and look afar. One who is ignorant and has heard little is mocked like the foolish and dull. As for the words called helpers: yan, zai, hu, ye.
keyLines.note: The conclusion. Time flies like an arrow and urges us on; the sun and moon keep shining. As a torch passes from one stick of firewood to another, so the one who cultivates blessings is kept safe and fortunate. Walk by the rules and carry yourself with dignity in the halls of state. Those who know little are mocked as simple. The text ends with four particles, 「焉哉乎也」, to show that the whole is at its end.

glossary.note: The vast, chaotic, unformed state of the earliest times.

glossary.en: ying ze - waxing, and slanting west
glossary.note: Ying is the full moon; ze is the sun leaning to the west (pronounced ze, fourth tone).
The old general word for the musical scale and its twelve pitches, matched to yin and yang.

glossary.en: run yu cheng sui - leap days make up the year
glossary.note: A lunar year is about 354 days, so the extra days that build up are put into a leap month to keep the seasons in step with the year.
In Buddhism the four elements of the body are earth, water, fire and wind. Another reading takes them as the Dao, Heaven, Earth and the king.
The five virtues: humaneness (ren), rightness (yi), ritual propriety (li), wisdom (zhi) and good faith (xin).
The common people; li means black. The Qin dynasty (221-206 BC) called the people 'black heads'.

glossary.en: qi and qi - two different characters
glossary.note: The qi of 'kin' and the qi of 'sorrow' are two distinct characters, which is how all thousand characters stay different.

main.background: The Thousand Character Classic was arranged by Zhou Xingsi by order of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty (502-557), one of the Southern Dynasties. It uses one thousand different characters to make 250 four-character rhyming lines. Tradition says Zhou Xingsi finished it in one night, and his hair had gone white by morning. Calligraphers such as Zhiyong, Huaisu and Zhao Mengfu all wrote it out, and it is an important text for learning calligraphy.
